findings.passage: When the story and the record diverged, the story won at least once.
findings.problem: This is the most damaging factual judgment about him in the piece, and it rests on a New York Times report that research never opened (only the Daily Wire summary and Wikipedia). The draft then goes further in the dent section ('his campaign reframed it instead of conceding'), reading an evasive motive into the campaign's answer. That answer (45 students were first placed in his room, then redistributed) could reconcile his line with year-level TEA class records. The draft does not say whether those records would capture a first-week placement. It also does not say whether he kept repeating the 45 figure after October 28, 2026. The former Rhodes teacher who said some classes reached 45 appears only as a one-line aside.
findings.acceptance_test: Either open the NYT piece and state exactly what the TEA records measure and whether he repeated the claim after publication, or reword both passages so they report only what is documented: his statement, the records, the campaign's account, and that the records cannot confirm or rule out the initial placement. Remove 'reframed it instead of conceding' and the 'story won' verdict unless the opened source supports them.

findings.passage: When principle and winning diverged, winning mostly won.
findings.problem: The lead sentence says he made a choice. The paragraph's own evidence shows a super PAC he could not legally direct, an opponent's hypocrisy charge relayed by a thin outlet (S13), and spending that Axios lumps together with his campaign's. The draft says no source shows whether he asked the PAC to stop, but it never says whether he or his campaign answered the hypocrisy charge. A reader comes away believing he picked winning over principle, which the record does not show.
findings.acceptance_test: Find and quote his or his campaign's response to the Crockett super PAC charge, or state that none was found in the sources checked. Rewrite the lead so it describes the situation (he benefited from outside spending he campaigns to ban) rather than a decision he is not shown to have made. Keep the legal caveat in the same paragraph, and split the $16 million into campaign and PAC spending if Axios allows it.

findings.passage: Talarico called it "a mischaracterization of a private conversation" and said he had "described Congressman Allred's method of campaigning as mediocre — but his life and service are not."
findings.problem: For a race-related allegation, the draft leaves out the core of his denial. The same CBS statement says "I would never attack him on the basis of race" and acknowledges how the remark could be heard. As written, the reader sees him admit the word 'mediocre' but never sees him deny the racial meaning, which is the actual allegation. CBS also reports the account came from a woman who said she had backed him and was now supporting Crockett. The 'In February 2026' date may also be early-February reporting of a TikTok posted earlier.
findings.acceptance_test: Add his explicit race denial ("I would never attack him on the basis of race") to the response, keep the 'unresolved' conclusion, and date the episode by the CBS report ("CBS News Texas reported on February 2, 2026") unless the TikTok's own date is confirmed.

findings.passage: Fourteen months later, Bartlett asked whether he could see himself running for president. "No."
findings.problem: This is cited as the clearest live test, but the transcript (Singju Post, 00:09:29–00:12:04) is more mixed. Asked a moment earlier why ministry would exclude a presidential run, he answered "It may not." Only the later direct question got "No… No, I really don't." In the same answer he gave reasons for the two-term pledge besides corruption: "other things that I want to do," "a well-balanced life," and handing "the reins over to someone else" with "fresh energy." The draft keeps only the self-preservation reason, and the description says he "capped his own Senate tenure" when he has only pledged to.
findings.acceptance_test: Give the presidency exchange accurately (a hedge, then a flat no to the direct question). Mention in a clause that his pledge also cites balance and turnover, not only corruption risk. Change 'capped his own Senate tenure' in the description to 'pledged to cap' or similar.

findings.passage: He takes office in January 2027 under exactly the pressure he says he does not trust himself to withstand.
findings.problem: This turns a remark about systems into a personal confession. His line ("the system eventually, unless it's reformed, will bring out the worst in all of us, including me") came while he was declining to judge individual politicians and arguing for systemic reform. He did not say he distrusts himself. The same stretch frames it as the fear "Talarico keeps describing," when the record supplied shows two remarks in one interview. Inference is fine, but here it is written as his own words.
findings.acceptance_test: Reword the closing sentence and the 'keeps describing' line so they follow what he actually said (the system will bring out the worst in everyone, including him), and say that the personal-fear reading is the author's. Alternatively, cite additional dated instances where he describes his own corruptibility.

findings.passage: In his telling, his aggression always arrives with a license: he is protecting someone and correcting a wrong.
findings.problem: 'Always' is an absolute drawn from a few self-told stories, and 'aggression' is a loaded word that none of the cited sources uses. The same pattern shows up in 'nobody could have banked on that in 2021' about seminary's brand value. That is an author's counterfactual, and it sits oddly with the draft's own report that he was publicly doing faith-based politics on a podcast in March 2021. Both sentences state as fact what are really the author's inferences.
findings.acceptance_test: Replace 'always' with a bounded claim ('in each of these stories') and use a less loaded noun, or support it. Cut 'nobody could have banked on that in 2021' or replace it with a sourced statement about how visible his faith was before he enrolled.

findings.passage: On August 9, 2021, The Texas Tribune counted at least four House Democrats back on the floor in Austin while most of their caucus stayed in Washington, D.C., holding out against a Republican voting bill.
findings.problem: The opened Tribune article does not say most of the caucus stayed in Washington. It refers to 'some' still there and to a group statement that 26 House Democrats would stay behind. Later, 'Rep. Gina Hinojosa named him' reads as if she singled him out, but she called out Fierro, González, Moody and Talarico together. Both details make him look more isolated than the source shows.
findings.acceptance_test: Change 'most of their caucus' to wording the Tribune supports (e.g., 'while a bloc of their colleagues stayed in Washington'). Say that Hinojosa named him alongside three other returning Democrats.

protected_passages.passage: The Daily Wire's headline called his whole origin story a lie, which the reporting does not show. It does show a story told bigger than the documents.
protected_passages.reason: Exactly the fairness move this role checks for: it corrects a hostile outlet's overreach and still keeps the real dent.

protected_passages.passage: A story repeated that often proves message discipline, not motive. What is useful is its shape.
protected_passages.reason: Clearly separates public record from inference on his most-repeated campaign story, without inventing a childhood wound.

protected_passages.passage: There is no recording and no second firsthand witness. It remains unresolved.
protected_passages.reason: Handles a sensitive single-source allegation honestly, with neither dismissal nor insinuation (pending subject-03's added denial).

protected_passages.passage: [FactCheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org/2026/09/paxtons-ai-heavy-ad-leaves-out-context-of-talarico-remarks-about-christianity/) restored what came next, after a Paxton ad stripped it out in 2026.
protected_passages.reason: Restores context to a quote that was clipped against him and dates the original remark before he had any statewide stakes. That is both fair and good evidence.

protected_passages.passage: Theft, sickness, corruption: the words come easily to him. Ones usually mean them. So do good preachers.
protected_passages.reason: A distinctive, honest limit on the type argument, letting the learned-register explanation stand next to the type.

assessment: Fairness proxy, not his voice. I reopened the Diary of a CEO transcript (Singju Post), the CBS News Texas allegation story and the 2021 Texas Tribune return story. The family-abuse account, the Paxton 'car keys' answer, the 'bring out the worst… including me' line and the 2021 return details are context-faithful. On the whole the draft separates record from inference well. It gives his responses on the nonbinary remark and the Daily Wire headline, and it leaves the 'mediocre Black man' allegation unresolved instead of insinuating. The weak spots are where the Type 3 case and the closing turn record into verdict. The 45-student 'story won' and 'reframed instead of conceding' rest on an unopened NYT piece, and the campaign's reconciling account goes untested. 'Winning mostly won' credits him with a super PAC decision no source shows, and his response to that charge is missing. The ending recasts a remark about systems as personal self-distrust. Smaller items: the race denial is missing from his allegation response, the presidency and term-limit answers are quoted selectively, there are a few absolute or loaded phrasings, and the opening overstates how isolated he was in 2021. Risks: the sensitive allegation (a racial remark from a private conversation) and contested typing (1 vs 3) both stand, so the expanded jury is warranted. The similarity advisory tripped on the boilerplate type-vocabulary line ('the three types whose core emotion is anger'); that is ordinary type vocabulary, not formulaic reuse, and not a fairness issue.
